name: Chiang Mai
note: The OG nomad hub. Best Nov–Mar. Avoid April smoke & May–Oct monsoon.
description: Chiang Mai is northern Thailand's largest city, 700 km north of Bangkok in the Thai highlands, with about 1.2 million people in its urban area. The old core is a moated square about a mile across, with the Ping River to the east and Doi Suthep to the west. Daily costs are low: a cappuccino is about ฿57, a cheap restaurant meal about ฿73 and a monthly transit pass ฿1,800 (Numbeo). Public transport is thin: songthaews, tuk-tuks, the RTC city bus (฿20 a ride) and Grab or Bolt. Most residents ride motorbikes. Coworkings include Punspace (Tha Phae Gate and Wiang Kaew, ฿3,899 a month), Yellow in Nimman (฿5,990) and Alt_ PingRiver in Wat Ket (฿4,000). Thailand's median fixed broadband is about 299 Mbps (Ookla, August 2026). Clocks follow ICT (UTC+7), and the DTV visa is aimed at remote workers. The climate is tropical savanna. December averages 29°C highs and 17°C lows, April peaks at 36.7°C, and August is the wettest month (223 mm). November to January is the most comfortable time to stay. Trade-offs: smoke from farm and forest burning, roughly February to April, often pushes fine-dust levels far above safe limits, and March is the worst month. Peak-hour traffic is heavy, and a central one-bedroom costs about ฿15,600 a month.

neighbourhoods.name: Nimmanhaemin (Nimman)
neighbourhoods.about: Cafe-lined sois between MAYA mall and Chiang Mai University
neighbourhoods.description: Nimmanhaemin Road runs south from the Rin Kham intersection, where MAYA Lifestyle Shopping Center opened in 2014, towards Suthep Road. Numbered sois branch off it on both sides, packed with cafes, small hotels, condos and the One Nimman shopping complex. This is the city's main base for remote workers. Yellow Coworking, Nim Space and The Social Club all sit in the area, and Chiang Mai University lies just to the west. In the evenings the bars fill with students from the university. A furnished one-bedroom here costs more than elsewhere in the city, and newer buildings sit at the top of the range. The main road and the Huay Kaew intersection get congested at peak hours.
watch_out: Pricier than other areas; traffic jams around the Rin Kham intersection
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Mostly walkable; Grab and Bolt cars are the easy way to the Old City, and red songthaews pass on Huay Kaew Road towards Doi Suthep.

neighbourhoods.name: Old City
neighbourhoods.about: Moated square of Lanna temples, guesthouses and weekend markets
neighbourhoods.description: The Old City is the square inside the moat and the remnants of the brick walls first laid out by King Mangrai in 1296. Wat Chedi Luang and Wat Phra Singh stand within a few minutes' walk of each other, and Tha Phae Gate on the east side is the main public gathering place. On Sunday evenings the Tha Phae Walking Street market fills Ratchadamnoen Road from the gate. Punspace runs two coworking branches here, at Tha Phae Gate and Wiang Kaew, and Buak Hat Park sits in the south-west corner. Housing is mostly guesthouses, serviced apartments and older low-rise buildings rather than modern condos, so rents are lower but quality and internet vary from building to building. Nightlife clusters near Tha Phae Gate.
watch_out: Few modern condos; internet quality varies by building
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Compact enough to walk; red songthaews and Grab cars cover trips beyond the moat, and the RTC city bus runs to the airport.

neighbourhoods.name: Santitham
neighbourhoods.about: Quiet residential sois north-east of Nimman, close to the moat
neighbourhoods.description: Santitham lies between Nimmanhaemin Road to the south-west, the Old City moat to the east and Chang Phueak to the north. Santitham Road runs through it, with rental buildings along Soi Santitham 2, 4 and 8 and the temple Wat Santitham. It is a residential area popular for long stays, with independent coffee shops and local restaurants rather than malls. The Chang Phueak night market, a well-known street-food stop, is at the northern edge, and Nimman's coworkings are a short ride away. One-bedrooms run roughly a third to a half cheaper than on Nimmanhaemin Road. The trade-off is plainer buildings: few have pools or gyms, and many landlords speak little English, though most use LINE.
watch_out: Older buildings; few pools or gyms
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Grab, Bolt and red songthaews reach Nimman and the Old City in minutes; Chang Phueak bus station for provincial routes is nearby.

neighbourhoods.name: Wat Ket (Riverside)
neighbourhoods.about: East bank of the Ping River, with riverside bars and newer condos
neighbourhoods.description: Wat Ket is the subdistrict on the east bank of the Ping River, across Nawarat Bridge from the Night Bazaar. It takes its name from Wat Ket Karam, a temple near the riverbank, and is mostly residential streets and small businesses. Charoen Rat Road, which follows the east bank, is one of the city's three busiest nightlife zones along with Tha Phae Gate and Loi Kroh Road. Alt_ PingRiver, a coworking space, charges about ฿4,000 a month, and the riverside has seen a run of newer condo developments. Those newer buildings make one-bedrooms here pricier than in the Old City. Nawarat Bridge is the main crossing towards the moat, so traffic backs up at peak hours, and the riverside bars can be loud at night.
watch_out: Riverside bars can be loud late at night
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Walk over Nawarat Bridge to the Night Bazaar and Warorot Market; Grab, Bolt and red songthaews cover the rest of town.

neighbourhoods.name: Chang Khlan (Night Bazaar)
neighbourhoods.about: Hotel district between the moat and the river, around the Night Bazaar
neighbourhoods.description: Chang Khlan lies east and south-east of the walled city along the west bank of the Ping River, with Chang Khlan Road running north to south through it. It holds many of the city's large hotels and the Night Bazaar, a handicraft and souvenir market between Tha Phae and Sridonchai roads. The area is also home to long-standing communities, notably Yunnanese Muslims. Warorot Market, the north's best-known market for local foods such as sai ua sausage and nam phrik num, is just north across Tha Phae Road. It is the most tourist-oriented part of town, which means plenty of hotel choice and evening activity, but also heavier traffic and prices aimed at visitors. Few long-stay condos are listed here compared with Nimman or Santitham.
watch_out: Tourist pricing around the Night Bazaar
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Walk to Tha Phae Gate or across Nawarat Bridge; Grab, Bolt and red songthaews run along Chang Khlan Road.

neighbourhoods.name: Suthep (Wat Umong & CMU)
neighbourhoods.about: Green edge of the city at the foot of Doi Suthep
neighbourhoods.description: Suthep is the subdistrict on the city's western edge, where it meets the forested slopes of Doi Suthep. Suthep Road runs out from Suan Dok Gate past Wat Suan Dok to Chiang Mai University, and Wat Umong, a 700-year-old forest temple with tunnels, sits about 1 km south of the main campus. The area is quieter and greener than Nimman, which lies just to the north-east. Wat Umong runs a meditation centre, and the Wat Pha Lat hiking trail up to Wat Phra That Doi Suthep starts near the university and the zoo. Daily life leans on the university, so many shops and cafes are aimed at students. Distances are longer and the lanes are less walkable, so most residents use a motorbike or ride-hailing.
watch_out: Spread out; you will want a scooter or Grab
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Red songthaews wait near the university's north gate and the zoo for Doi Suthep; Grab and Bolt cover trips into Nimman and the Old City.

neighbourhoods.name: Hang Dong
neighbourhoods.about: Southern suburb of houses, gardens and Ban Tawai woodcarving
neighbourhoods.description: Hang Dong is the district immediately south of Mueang Chiang Mai, part of the city's urban sprawl. It is known as the first place in Thailand where longan was grown, and the village of Ban Tawai in Khun Khong subdistrict has been a woodcarving and handicraft centre since the 1960s. People choose it for space: houses with gardens, and at the top end modern homes with private pools, at prices that would buy a small condo in Nimman. It suits families and people who want quiet more than cafes on the doorstep. It is car or scooter country. Shops, coworkings and the Old City are a drive away, public transport is limited to yellow songthaews towards San Patong, and smoke in burning season affects the valley as much as the city.
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Yellow songthaews run between the city and Hang Dong and San Patong; otherwise plan on a car, scooter or Grab.

neighbourhoods.name: Nimman
neighbourhoods.about: Cafés & cowork — nomad HQ

neighbourhoods.name: Nimmanhaemin Rd
neighbourhoods.about: Hip restaurants, bars & yoga

coworking: CAMP at Maya Mall – free wifi+coffee
best_season: Nov–Feb (cool and dry). Avoid late Feb–Apr: crop-burning smoky season can make the air unhealthy.
flight_from_miami: ≈24–27h with one stop (via Tokyo, Seoul, Taipei or Hong Kong) to CNX.
time_zone: UTC+7 — 11–12h ahead of US Eastern. US work calls land late at night.
sim_cost: AIS or TrueMove ≈ $8–12/mo with 20–50 GB. Coverage excellent.

getting_around: Songthaew trucks, Grab, and scooter rentals; the centre is walkable.
scene: Legendary — one of the original global nomad hubs, dense with coworkings and meetups.

name: Bangkok
note: Best Oct–Feb. Excellent transit hub. Hot year-round.
description: Thailand's capital sits on the Chao Phraya River, with the Grand Palace and old temples on Rattanakosin Island and newer towers along Sukhumvit, Silom and Sathon. It is a city of distinct districts rather than one centre. A month here is cheap by big-city standards: a cappuccino is about ฿94, a basic restaurant meal about ฿100 and a monthly transit pass about ฿1,180. The BTS Skytrain and MRT lines, plus river express boats, cover most central areas. Coworkings such as The Hive (Thong Lo), JustCo (AIA Sathorn) and Spaces (Asok) charge roughly ฿3,500–8,000 a month for a hot desk. Thailand's median fixed broadband runs near 370 Mbps. Clocks follow ICT (UTC+7), and the DTV visa is aimed at remote workers. The climate is tropical: hot all year, with an average high of 35.7°C in April. The rainy season runs from mid-May to October, wettest in September; November to February is drier and the easiest time to arrive. Trade-offs: heat and humidity most of the year, heavy road traffic (Asok carries about three times its design capacity), and a central one-bedroom around ฿22,700 a month.

neighbourhoods.name: Sukhumvit (Asok & Nana)
neighbourhoods.about: Transit hub of malls, offices and side-street condos around Asok
neighbourhoods.description: Asok is the junction of Sukhumvit Road and Asok Montri Road (Soi 21), where the BTS Sukhumvit Line meets the MRT Blue Line. The streets around it, west towards Nana and east towards Phrom Phong, are lined with office towers, condos, hotels and the Terminal 21 shopping centre. Sukhumvit is where many foreigners in Bangkok live, and the corridor has some of the city's densest choice of coworking spaces, including Spaces at Exchange Tower near Asok. Benchasiri Park, on Sukhumvit Road near Phrom Phong, is the nearest larger green space. Being on two rail lines makes it the easiest base for getting around without taxis. The trade-off is the road itself: Asok Montri Road carries far more traffic than it was built for, and the main road is loud and busy day and night.
watch_out: Asok junction is one of the most congested in the city
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Asok (BTS Sukhumvit Line) connects to Sukhumvit station on the MRT Blue Line; Nana and Phrom Phong BTS are one stop either side.

neighbourhoods.name: Thong Lo & Ekkamai
neighbourhoods.about: Restaurant and bar sois off Sukhumvit with a big Japanese community
neighbourhoods.description: Thong Lo is Soi Sukhumvit 55, running north from Thong Lo BTS station to Phetchaburi Road in Watthana District. Ekkamai (Soi 63) runs parallel one station east. Once an area of car dealerships, Thong Lo turned into a street of boutiques, restaurants and cocktail bars from the early 2000s. A large Japanese community lives here, and both streets are lined with condos, cafés, bars and embassies. Time Out ranked Ekkamai among the world's coolest neighbourhoods for its cafés, nightlife and restaurants. The Hive coworking is on Sukhumvit Soi 49 and The Campus is in Ekkamai. The sois are long, so places far up Thong Lo or Ekkamai are a motorbike-taxi or bus ride from the BTS. It suits longer stays, food-focused travellers and anyone who wants nightlife nearby but a residential base.
watch_out: Long sois: the far ends are a ride, not a walk, from the BTS
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Thong Lo and Ekkamai stations are on the BTS Sukhumvit Line; a Khlong Saen Saep express boat pier sits at the north end of Thong Lo.

neighbourhoods.name: Silom & Sathorn
neighbourhoods.about: Business district between Lumphini Park and the river
neighbourhoods.description: Si Lom Road and the parallel Sathon Road form one of Bangkok's main business districts in Bang Rak and Sathon. Silom was one of the city's first modern roads, built along a canal in the 1860s; its name is usually traced to a windmill that once stood there. Sathon is lined with bank headquarters, 40-storey condos and several embassies, while Silom's side streets mix older communities with shopping and nightlife. Lumphini Park, a 360-rai park with a lake, sits where Silom meets Rama IV Road. JustCo has a space at AIA Sathorn Tower. Office crowds make weekdays busy and some streets quiet at weekends. It works well for business travellers and anyone who wants rail links in two directions and the park nearby.
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Sala Daeng (BTS Silom Line) links to Si Lom (MRT Blue Line); Chong Nonsi and Surasak BTS serve Sathon, with Lumphini MRT at its east end.

neighbourhoods.name: Ari
neighbourhoods.about: Residential soi of cafés and bakeries north of the centre
neighbourhoods.description: Ari (also spelled Aree) is a residential neighbourhood in Phaya Thai District, centred on Soi Ari (Phahonyothin Soi 7) in an area locally called Sanam Pao. In the 1950s and 1960s it was a quiet area of old families and government officials. Today the soi is lined with cafés, bakeries, restaurants and a community-style mall, and media including The New York Times have listed it among the world's best neighbourhoods. Several ministries and the Public Relations Department have offices at the far end of the soi. It is cheaper and calmer than Sukhumvit, with Chatuchak Weekend Market a few BTS stops north. Nightlife is limited, and reaching the old town or river takes a change of line. Good for long stays and remote work on a budget.
watch_out: Few bars; the old town and river are 30+ minutes away
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Ari station (N5) on the BTS Sukhumvit Line sits at the entrance to Soi Ari on Phahonyothin Road.

neighbourhoods.name: Chinatown (Yaowarat)
neighbourhoods.about: Gold shops, markets and one of the city's best-known food streets
neighbourhoods.description: Yaowarat Road, built between 1892 and 1900, is the main artery of Bangkok's Chinatown in Samphanthawong District. Chinese traders settled here after moving from the site of the Grand Palace, and the district now spreads over Charoen Krung, Song Wat and Ratchawong roads. By day the area trades in gold, textiles, spare parts and dried goods, with the narrow Sampheng market at its centre; it has been described as having more gold shops than anywhere else. At night Yaowarat becomes a large food street. Wat Traimit, home of a large gold Buddha, is at the eastern end. Streets are crowded and narrow, and evenings are noisy. Wat Mangkon MRT station makes it easy to reach. Good for short stays, food and photography.
watch_out: Crowded, narrow streets and late-night noise along Yaowarat
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Wat Mangkon station on the MRT Blue Line is in Samphanthawong, close to Yaowarat Road.

neighbourhoods.name: Old Town & Banglamphu
neighbourhoods.about: Palace, temples and riverside lanes on and around Rattanakosin Island
neighbourhoods.description: Rattanakosin Island in Phra Nakhon District is the historic core, bounded by the Chao Phraya River and old moat canals. It holds the Grand Palace, residence of the kings of Siam since 1782, and Wat Pho with its reclining Buddha. Bang Lamphu covers the area north of the palace, from Phra Athit Road to Samsen Road. It grew around a canal pier and market, and Khaosan Road, a 410-metre street built in 1892, sits about 1 km north of the Grand Palace. Phra Athit Road runs along the river with piers and a park around Phra Sumen Fort. Most sights are within walking distance, and the river boat is the quickest link south. The trade-offs: no BTS, slower trips to the business districts, and backpacker noise around Khaosan.
watch_out: No BTS line; Khaosan Road is loud late at night
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Sanam Chai station (MRT Blue Line) serves the palace area; Chao Phraya Express Boat piers line Phra Athit Road.

neighbourhoods.name: Charoen Krung Riverside
neighbourhoods.about: Bangkok's first modern road, riverside hotels and old trading houses
neighbourhoods.description: Charoen Krung Road, built in 1862–64, was the first road in Thailand made with modern methods. Its stretch through Bang Rak, along the east bank of the Chao Phraya, once served the city's European trading community and consulates. Historic buildings remain, including Assumption Cathedral, the principal Catholic church of Thailand, on Oriental Avenue. The riverbank here holds several of the city's best-known hotels, and the Sathorn express-boat pier is the hub of the river boat network. Rooms on the river are expensive, and the area is a walk or boat ride from the rail network rather than on top of it. It suits couples, luxury stays and anyone who wants to use the river to get around.
watch_out: Only one BTS station; many spots need a walk or boat
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Saphan Taksin (BTS Silom Line) sits beside Sathorn pier, the central stop of the Chao Phraya Express Boat.
